“könnte” = “KØN-teh” (could, would be able to), “konnte” = “KON-teh” (was able to). The umlaut changes the meaning!
With “Könnten Sie…?” your voice rises slightly at the end, and “bitte” is said warmly, not curtly.
Konjunktiv II is the “would mood”. For A2 you need four forms. They all look like the Präteritum, but they have an UMLAUT:

The umlaut makes the difference: “ich hatte” = I had / “ich hätte” = I would have. “ich konnte” = I could (was able to) / “ich könnte” = I could (would be able to). “wurde” = became / “würde” = would (do).
The same goes for: müssen → müsste, dürfen → dürfte, sollen → sollte (no umlaut), wissen → wüsste.
The more “hypothetical” the request, the more polite it is:
Machen Sie bitte das Fenster auf.
Würden Sie bitte das Fenster aufmachen?
At the café, the bakery or the counter, “Ich hätte gern…” is the most elegant phrase: “Ich hätte gern zwei Brötchen, bitte.”

Word order: “würde” in position 2, the infinitive at the end (as with modals and the future).

With “würde” you can form the Konjunktiv II of almost any verb: “Ich würde gern reisen / tanzen / schlafen”. Exceptions: with sein, haben and the modals their own forms are preferred (wäre, hätte, könnte).

Mara needed time to think about the contract. She rang her parents. Her mother said: “We'd love to see you more often. But we want you to be happy.” Her father just said: “Bees fly far from home too. But they always know where the hive is.” Mara understood what he meant.

One Sunday evening in September she was sitting with Ludwig, Lena and the twins in the courtyard, under the fairy lights that nobody had taken down since the courtyard party. The chestnut tree was already dropping its first brown chestnuts onto the table. Kuba was collecting them in a bag.
I have an idea. Everyone says one wish. Something they'd like to do if they could. Honestly.
I'd love to have a dog of my own. A dachshund. Like Fritz. But Mum says the flat is too small.
I'd love to have two weeks' holiday in one go. No alarm clock at four. And…
She looked at her phone, where a message from Andrei was glowing, and blushed. “And I'm not saying the other one.” They all laughed.

Ludwig looked for a long time at the yellow lamp in his window. Then he said quietly: “I'd love to drive the M1 one more time. Not as a passenger. At the front, as the driver. One more time through Prenzlauer Berg, the whole route. That would be my wish.”

From above, from the open window on the fourth floor, came a voice. Mrs Hoffmann had heard everything. “And I,” she called, “would love to sing in a real concert hall one more time. In front of an audience. Not just for the courtyard.” Then she closed the window, as if she had said too much.
That night Mara couldn't sleep. She was thinking about wishes. A dog, a holiday, a tram, a concert hall. Some were impossible. But perhaps not all of them.

The next day, after the early shift, she didn't go home but to the tram museum of the Berlin transport company, in the depot in Niederschönhausen. She had read online that there were old trams there, vintage vehicles, which you could hire for special trips. An older man with a moustache and a blue uniform jacket came to meet her.
Good afternoon. Excuse me, could you help me? I have an unusual request.

She told him about Ludwig. About the forty years on the M1 line, about the night in November 1989 when he stopped the tram and crossed the border on foot, about the yellow lamp from the flea market. The man listened and said nothing. Then he asked: “What's your friend's name?”

The man took off his glasses and wiped them for a long time. “Ludwig Brandt,” he said at last. “Ludwig with the guitar? I was his apprentice. In 1985. He taught me how to drive a Tatra through the snow without the passengers falling over. He always used to say: You don't drive a tram with your hands. You drive it with your gut.”

His name was Mr Wolff and he was now the director of the museum. He said there was an old yellow Tatra tram in the depot, exactly like the one Ludwig used to drive. It ran once a month for tourists. “A seventy-eight-year-old driver isn't allowed to drive on his own, of course,” he said. “That would be against all the rules. But if I sat next to him… and if we did it early on a Sunday morning, when the route is clear…”

Mr Wolff led Mara through the large, cool hall of the depot. It smelled of oil, metal and old wood. On the tracks stood trams from a hundred years: a small open one from 1910 with wooden benches, a red-and-white one from the fifties, and right at the back, in the light of a tall window, a yellow Tatra with round headlights at the front that looked like two friendly eyes. On the side was the number 5218.

This tram ran on the M1 line until 1992, which back then was still called line 46. It's quite possible that Ludwig drove exactly this car. We have the old timetables in the archive. If you like, I could check.

Mara put her hand on the cold yellow metal. She imagined Ludwig standing here at the front fifty years ago, young, with long hair, his guitar in the little locker, driving every morning at five through the dark, quiet streets of Prenzlauer Berg. Past the stop in front of the bakery, which back then wasn't a bakery yet but a small greengrocer's. Perhaps, she thought, Ingrid had waited for him here for three days.
Young lady, without Ludwig Brandt I wouldn't be here today. Of course I'd do it. But don't tell him anything. It has to be a surprise.

On the way home, on the M1, Mara sat right at the front, directly behind the driver, and looked through the big windscreen at the tracks stretching through Prenzlauer Berg. She thought about Ludwig, Mrs Hoffmann, Kuba, Lena. And suddenly she knew the answer to Ms Schreiber's question. She would stay. There were still too many wishes here that someone had to fulfil.

When she got off at her stop, she saw the yellow lamp lit up on the first floor. She smiled. Ludwig didn't know anything yet. And that was a good thing. Some wishes are most beautiful when they come unexpectedly.
